shared_text:
The flight. A narrow-body airliner on approach. Daytime, with cloud ceilings of 2,000–2,500 ft.

The crew. The captain was the pilot flying and the first officer the pilot monitoring, on their first day together; the captain had chosen to fly every leg.

What happened. Earlier, the captain had made a radio call, begun setting the minimums before clearance until reminded by the first officer, selected flaps personally, and called for flaps 40 at 4–5 knots above the limit speed; the first officer waited for the speed to drop. As the aircraft left 2,500 ft near the final approach fix, ATC reported a conflict with a slower single-engine aircraft and offered a vector to resequence. The first officer accepted, reading back a heading and "maintain 2,500 ft". Treating this as a go-around, the captain pressed the take-off/go-around switches; the first officer recalled no standard callout. The aircraft accelerated quickly and climbed slightly; the captain called for flaps 15, then gear up. Still on runway heading, the first officer selected heading mode and prompted the turn; the captain began a left turn. When the first officer noted the speed was above the flaps 15 limit, the captain called for retraction on schedule. After flaps 5, the bank angle alert sounded at about 40 degrees. The first officer called "bank angle"; the captain applied more left roll, and the first officer took the control column and helped roll the aircraft back to wings level; it was nose-low and descending rapidly.
safe_outcome: ATC issued a low-altitude warning. The descent was stopped at about 2,000 ft, 1,200–1,300 ft above the ground, and the aircraft climbed back to 2,500–2,700 ft. The autothrottles and autopilot were re-engaged, and the crew flew an approach to another runway and landed normally. After landing the crew recorded a flaps 5 overspeed of about 10 knots, and maintenance was called to inspect the flaps. There was no further conflict with the single-engine aircraft or other traffic. No one was hurt and no aircraft was damaged.
bad_outcome: Another aircraft was crossing nearby. Both crews received TCAS resolution advisories and followed them, and the aircraft passed about 300 feet vertically and half a mile apart. A flight attendant on this aircraft was thrown against a galley cart during the manoeuvre and received a minor injury.
notes: Removed under rule 3: the first officer's 'Cause' section (normalisation of deviance, blurred duties, sharing the blame, the captain's manner, soft go-around training) and 'To my surprise'; the captain's retrospective view that altitude hold and level change would have been better, and 'things happen very quickly'. Kept: the captain's understanding at the time that ATC wanted a go-around (captain's narrative), alongside the first officer's account of the instruction actually read back. Moved under rule 5: ATC's low-altitude warning, the height at which the descent was stopped, the climb back, re-engaging the automation, the landing on another runway, and the logbook entry and flap inspection. Removed under rule 6: airport, runway and fix names; the single-engine aircraft's type. Compressed or cut for length: the earlier approach actions (the captain's radio call requesting vectors, setting the minimums before clearance, selecting flaps 25 and 30, flaps 40 called 4–5 knots fast) are kept in one sentence; cut are the captain's shallow vertical-speed descent and doubt whether VNAV would capture the path, and the first officer's 'positive rate' call. Left out as after the outcome and differing between versions: the first officer reducing thrust as the speed again neared the limit, and the captain's large control inputs delaying autopilot engagement. Judgement calls: the narratives differ on whether the single-engine aircraft was landing on the same runway (captain) or a parallel runway (first officer); the text says only 'a slower single-engine aircraft'. Deviation D4: the report shows a traffic conflict (ATC's call), so the standard 'no conflict' line would contradict the shared text; the safe ending says there was no further conflict and ends 'no aircraft was damaged'. The report does not say whether the flap inspection found damage; the frozen 'no aircraft was damaged' is used. Bracket 'crossing': the aircraft turned off the approach path at low height near other approach traffic; 'descending' would also fit, since the reported traffic was on approach.
